facts.quote: authority: Mantell, 1827

facts.statement: Megalosaurus lived during the Middle Jurassic, specifically the Bathonian age, approximately 166 million years ago.
facts.quote: lived during the Middle Jurassic (Bathonian age, ~166 million years ago)

facts.statement: Megalosaurus lived in what is now southern England.
facts.quote: in what is now southern England

facts.statement: The earliest remains of Megalosaurus were described in the 17th century.
facts.quote: The earliest remains of Megalosaurus were described in the 17th century

facts.statement: William Buckland named the genus Megalosaurus in 1824.
facts.quote: Megalosaurus was named in 1824 by William Buckland

facts.statement: The type species M. bucklandii was named in 1827 by Gideon Mantell in honor of William Buckland.
facts.quote: named in 1827 by Gideon Mantell, after Buckland

facts.statement: Richard Owen used Megalosaurus as one of the three genera to define the group Dinosauria in 1842.
facts.quote: In 1842, Megalosaurus was one of three genera on which Richard Owen based his Dinosauria

facts.statement: Megalosaurus was approximately 6 meters long and weighed about 700 kilograms.
facts.quote: Megalosaurus was about 6 m long, weighing about 700 kg

facts.statement: Megalosaurus was a bipedal dinosaur that walked on stout hindlimbs.
facts.quote: It was bipedal, walking on stout hindlimbs

facts.statement: Megalosaurus had short but very robust forelimbs.
facts.quote: Its forelimbs were short, though very robust

facts.statement: Megalosaurus had a large head equipped with long, curved teeth.
facts.quote: Megalosaurus had a rather large head, equipped with long curved teeth

facts.statement: Edward Lhuyd described a fossil tooth in 1699, which he believed to be from a fish.
facts.quote: In 1699, Edward Lhuyd described what he believed to have been a fish tooth

facts.statement: The fossil specimen OU 1328, potentially a Megalosaurus tooth, has been lost.
facts.quote: OU 1328 has since been lost

facts.statement: The fossil specimen OU 1328 was collected near Caswell, Oxfordshire, during the 17th century.
facts.quote: OU 1328 was collected near Caswell, near Witney, Oxfordshire sometime during the 17th century

facts.statement: A fragment of a bone was recovered from the Taynton Limestone Formation in Oxfordshire in 1676.
facts.quote: Part of a bone was recovered from the Taynton Limestone Formation of Stonesfield limestone quarry, Oxfordshire in 1676

facts.statement: Robert Plot published a description and illustration of a dinosaur bone fragment in 1676.
facts.quote: Sir Thomas Pennyson gave the fragment to naturalist Robert Plot, who published a description and illustration in his Natural History of Oxfordshire in 1676

facts.statement: The illustration by Robert Plot was the first published illustration of a dinosaur bone.
facts.quote: It was the first illustration of a dinosaur bone published

facts.statement: Robert Plot correctly identified the fossil fragment as the lower part of a femur from a large animal.
facts.quote: Plot correctly identified the bone as the lower extremity of the thighbone or femur of a large animal

facts.statement: Robert Plot initially thought the bone belonged to a Roman war elephant and later to a giant human.
facts.quote: He therefore at first concluded it to be the thigh bone of a Roman war elephant and later that of a giant human

facts.statement: It is debated whether the name "Scrotum humanum" was assigned by Richard Brookes or resulted from an illustrator's error.
facts.quote: However, it is possible that the attribution of this name stemmed from illustrator error, not Richard Brookes

facts.statement: The ICZN concluded that "Scrotum humanum" was not a valid scientific name because it was published only as an illustration label.
facts.quote: concluding that the term "Scrotum humanum", published merely as a label for an illustration, did not constitute the valid creation of a new name

facts.statement: It is debated whether the femur fragment can be definitively assigned to Megalosaurus rather than a different contemporary theropod.
facts.quote: Furthermore, the partial femur was too incomplete to definitely be referred to Megalosaurus and not a different, contemporary theropod

facts.statement: Today, M. bucklandii is considered the only valid species of Megalosaurus, as other species assigned to the genus are not directly related to it.
facts.quote: Today it is understood that none of these additional species was directly related to M. bucklandii, which is the only true Megalosaurus species

facts.statement: A partial lower jaw of Megalosaurus was discovered about 40 feet underground in a Stonesfield Slate mine in the early 1790s.
facts.quote: It was discovered about 40 ft underground in a Stonesfield Slate mine during the early 1790s

facts.statement: The geological layers containing Megalosaurus fossils are part of the Taynton Limestone Formation and date to the mid-Bathonian stage of the Jurassic Period.
facts.quote: The layers there are currently considered part of the Taynton Limestone Formation, dating to the mid-Bathonian stage of the Jurassic Period

facts.statement: Megalosaurus was the first non-avian dinosaur genus to be named.
facts.quote: Megalosaurus was the first non-avian dinosaur genus named

facts.statement: In 1990, Ralph Molnar selected the dentary (front part of the lower jaw), specimen OUM J13505, as the lectotype for Megalosaurus.
facts.quote: In 1990, Ralph Molnar chose the famous dentary (front part of the lower jaw), OUM J13505, as such a lectotype

facts.statement: William Buckland classified Megalosaurus as a giant animal belonging to Sauria, a group of lizards that at the time included crocodiles.
facts.quote: Buckland identified the organism as being a giant animal belonging to the Sauria – the Lizards, at the time seen as including the crocodiles

facts.statement: William Buckland estimated that Megalosaurus was 12 meters long in life, repeating an estimate made by Georges Cuvier.
facts.quote: repeating an estimate by Cuvier that the largest pieces he described, indicated an animal 12 meters long in life

facts.statement: In 1827, Gideon Mantell assigned the valid binomial name Megalosaurus bucklandii to the species.
facts.quote: In 1827, Gideon Mantell included Megalosaurus in his geological survey of southeastern England, and assigned the species its current valid binomial name, Megalosaurus bucklandii

facts.statement: The variant name Megalosaurus bucklandi was first published in 1832 by Christian Erich Hermann von Meyer.
facts.quote: Until recently, the form Megalosaurus bucklandi was often used, a variant first published in 1832 by Christian Erich Hermann von Meyer

facts.statement: It is generally considered that the name Megalosaurus announced by James Parkinson in 1822 was a nomen nudum.
facts.quote: It is generally considered that the name in 1822 was still a nomen nudum ("naked name")

facts.statement: The fossils originally described by Buckland formed a syntype series because they represented several different individuals.
facts.quote: Because they represented several individuals, the described fossils formed a syntype series

facts.statement: William Buckland produced the first reconstruction of Megalosaurus.
facts.quote: The first reconstruction was given by Buckland himself.

facts.statement: William Buckland originally considered Megalosaurus to be a quadruped.
facts.quote: He considered Megalosaurus to be a quadruped.

facts.statement: Buckland described Megalosaurus as an amphibian capable of swimming and walking on land.
facts.quote: He thought it was an "amphibian", i.e. an animal capable of both swimming in the sea and walking on land.

facts.statement: Buckland imagined Megalosaurus resembling a gigantic lizard.
facts.quote: Generally, in his mind Megalosaurus resembled a gigantic lizard

facts.statement: Buckland noted that the thigh bone shape suggested Megalosaurus held its legs upright rather than sprawling.
facts.quote: Buckland already understood from the form of the thigh bone head that the legs were not so much sprawling as held rather upright.

facts.statement: In 1824, Buckland estimated Megalosaurus was 40 feet long and weighed as much as a seven-foot-tall elephant.
facts.quote: In the original description of 1824, Buckland repeated Cuvier's size estimate that Megalosaurus would have been 40 feet long with the weight of a seven foot tall elephant.

facts.statement: Buckland was hurried into naming Megalosaurus after seeing a fossil thigh bone twice as long as the one he had described.
facts.quote: Buckland had also been hurried into naming his new reptile by a visit he had made to the fossil collection of Mantell, who during the lecture announced to have acquired a fossil thigh bone of enormous magnitude, twice as long as that just described.

facts.statement: The large thigh bone that influenced Buckland's size estimates is now known to belong to Iguanodon or an iguanodontid, not Megalosaurus.
facts.quote: Today, this is known to have belonged to Iguanodon, or at least some iguanodontid, but at the time both men assumed this bone belonged to Megalosaurus also.

facts.statement: Buckland revised his estimate to a maximum length of 60 to 70 feet in the printed version of his lecture.
facts.quote: Even taking into account the effects of allometry, heavier animals having relatively stouter bones, Buckland was forced in the printed version of his lecture to estimate the maximum length of Megalosaurus at 60 to 70 feet.

facts.statement: The existence of Megalosaurus created a conflict with Christian orthodoxy regarding the origin of suffering and death.
facts.quote: The existence of Megalosaurus posed some problems for Christian orthodoxy, which typically held that suffering and death had only come into the world through Original Sin, which seemed irreconcilable with the presence of a gigantic devouring reptile during a pre-Adamitic phase of history.

facts.statement: Buckland argued that Megalosaurus played a beneficial role by killing old and sick animals to reduce suffering.
facts.quote: Buckland rejected the usual solution, that such carnivores would originally have been peaceful vegetarians, as infantile and claimed in one of the Bridgewater Treatises that Megalosaurus had played a beneficial role in creation by ending the lives of old and ill animals, "to diminish the aggregate amount of animal suffering".

facts.statement: Richard Owen claimed on August 2, 1841, that certain prehistoric reptiles had reached the organizational level of mammals.
facts.quote: In reaction, on 2 August 1841 Richard Owen during a lecture to the British Association for the Advancement of Science claimed that certain prehistoric reptilian groups had already attained the organisational level of present mammals, implying there had been no progress.

facts.statement: Richard Owen cited Megalosaurus as an example of a higher-level reptile.
facts.quote: Owen presented three examples of such higher level reptiles: Iguanodon, Hylaeosaurus and Megalosaurus.

facts.statement: Richard Owen estimated the total body length of Megalosaurus at 30 feet.
facts.quote: By simply adding the known length of the vertebrae, instead of extrapolating from a lizard, Owen arrived at a total body length for Megalosaurus of 30 feet.

facts.statement: Richard Owen established the group Dinosauria in 1842, including Megalosaurus.
facts.quote: In the printed version of the lecture published in 1842, Owen united the three reptiles into a separate group: the Dinosauria.

facts.statement: Megalosaurus was one of the three original dinosaurs defined by Richard Owen.
facts.quote: Megalosaurus was thus one of the three original dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins built a life-sized concrete model of Megalosaurus for the Crystal Palace Park in 1852.
facts.quote: In 1852, Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins was commissioned to build a life-sized concrete model of Megalosaurus for the exhibition of prehistoric animals at the Crystal Palace Park in Sydenham, where it remains to this day.

facts.statement: The Crystal Palace model depicted Megalosaurus as a mammal-like quadruped based on Owen's ideas.
facts.quote: Hawkins worked under the direction of Owen and the statue reflected Owen's ideas that Megalosaurus would have been a mammal-like quadruped.

facts.statement: The Crystal Palace model features a shoulder hump, possibly inspired by vertebral spines Owen acquired in the early 1850s.
facts.quote: The sculpture in Crystal Palace Park shows a conspicuous hump on the shoulders and it has been suggested this was inspired by a set of high vertebral spines acquired by Owen in the early 1850s.

facts.statement: Vertebral spines once referred to Megalosaurus are now classified as a separate genus, Becklespinax.
facts.quote: Today, they are seen as a separate genus Becklespinax, but Owen referred them to Megalosaurus.

facts.statement: The discovery of Compsognathus in 1859 challenged the idea that carnivorous dinosaurs like Megalosaurus were quadrupeds.
facts.quote: The presumption that carnivorous dinosaurs, like Megalosaurus, were quadrupeds was first challenged by the find of Compsognathus in 1859.

facts.statement: The type specimen of Eustreptospondylus, discovered near Oxford in 1870, was the first reasonably intact large theropod skeleton and was clearly bipedal.
facts.quote: In 1870, near Oxford, the type specimen of Eustreptospondylus was discovered – the first reasonably intact skeleton of a large theropod. It was clearly bipedal.

facts.statement: The Oxford University Museum of Natural History display contains most specimens from Buckland's original Megalosaurus description.
facts.quote: The Oxford University Museum of Natural History display contains most of the specimens from the original description by Buckland.

facts.statement: Stonesfield quarries produced Megalosaurus bucklandii fossils until 1911, mostly consisting of pelvis and hindlimb bones.
facts.quote: The quarries at Stonesfield, which were worked until 1911, continued to produce Megalosaurus bucklandii fossils, mostly single bones from the pelvis and hindlimbs.

facts.statement: Vertebrae and skull bones of Megalosaurus are rare finds.
facts.quote: Vertebrae and skull bones are rare.

facts.statement: In 2010, Roger Benson counted 103 Megalosaurus specimens from the Stonesfield Slate representing at least seven individuals.
facts.quote: In 2010, Roger Benson counted a total of 103 specimens from the Stonesfield Slate, from a minimum of seven individuals.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the Stonesfield material represents a single taxon.
facts.quote: It has been contentious whether this material represents just a single taxon.

facts.statement: Julia Day and Paul Barrett claimed in 2004 that two morphotypes of Megalosaurus existed based on thighbone differences.
facts.quote: In 2004, Julia Day and Paul Barrett claimed that there were two morphotypes present, based on small differences in the thighbones.

facts.statement: Roger Benson initially favored the two-morphotype idea in 2008 but concluded the differences were illusory in 2010.
facts.quote: In 2008 Benson favoured this idea, but in 2010 concluded the differences were illusory.

facts.statement: Thomas Huxley assigned maxilla fragment OUM J13506 to M. bucklandii in 1869.
facts.quote: A maxilla fragment, specimen OUM J13506, was, in 1869 assigned, by Thomas Huxley, to M. bucklandii.

facts.statement: Remains found in the Chipping Norton Limestone Formation dating to the early Bathonian were referred to Megalosaurus in 1939.
facts.quote: Apart from the finds in the Taynton Limestone Formation, in 1939 Sidney Hugh Reynolds referred remains to Megalosaurus that had been found in the older Chipping Norton Limestone Formation dating from the early Bathonian, about 30 single teeth and bones.

facts.statement: In 2009, Benson affirmed that remains from the New Park Quarry belonged to M. bucklandii despite age disparities.
facts.quote: Though the age disparity makes it problematic to assume an identity with Megalosaurus bucklandii, in 2009 Benson could not establish any relevant anatomical differences with M. bucklandii among the remains found at one site, the New Park Quarry, and therefore affirmed the reference to that species.

facts.statement: Material from the Oakham Quarry contained an ilium that was clearly dissimilar to M. bucklandii.
facts.quote: However, in another site, the Oakham Quarry, the material contained one bone, an ilium, that was clearly dissimilar.

facts.statement: Trace fossils have sometimes been referred to Megalosaurus or the ichnogenus Megalosauripus.
facts.quote: Sometimes trace fossils have been referred to Megalosaurus or to the ichnogenus Megalosauripus.

facts.statement: A group of fossilized footprints was found in a limestone quarry at Ardley in 1997.
facts.quote: In 1997, a famous group of fossilized footprints (ichnites) was found in a limestone quarry at Ardley, 20 kilometers northeast of Oxford.

facts.statement: The footprints found at Ardley were thought to have been made by Megalosaurus and possibly Cetiosaurus.
facts.quote: They were thought to have been made by Megalosaurus and possibly also some left by Cetiosaurus.

facts.statement: One of the footprints showed a theropod accelerating from walking to running.
facts.quote: One track was of a theropod accelerating from walking to running.

facts.statement: Roger Benson argued that referring footprints to Megalosaurus is unprovable because they lack unique traits.
facts.quote: According to Benson, such referrals are unprovable, as the tracks show no traits unique to Megalosaurus.

facts.statement: Finds from sites outside England, especially in France, were referred to M. bucklandii in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
facts.quote: Finds from sites outside England, especially in France, have in the nineteenth and twentieth century been referred to M. bucklandii.

facts.statement: No complete skeleton of Megalosaurus has been found despite many bone discoveries.
facts.quote: Since the first finds, many other Megalosaurus bones have been recovered; however, no complete skeleton has yet been found.

facts.statement: The details of Megalosaurus's physical appearance cannot be certain due to the lack of a complete skeleton.
facts.quote: Therefore, the details of its physical appearance cannot be certain.

facts.statement: A full osteology of all known Megalosaurus material was published in 2010 by Benson.
facts.quote: However, a full osteology of all known material was published in 2010 by Benson.

facts.statement: Megalosaurus was a bipedal animal with a horizontal torso balanced by a long horizontal tail.
facts.quote: It was bipedal, the horizontal torso being balanced by a long horizontal tail.

facts.statement: Megalosaurus had long, strong hindlimbs with three forward-facing weight-bearing toes and relatively short but robust forelimbs that probably carried three digits.
facts.quote: The hindlimbs were long and strong with three forward-facing weight-bearing toes, the forelimbs relatively short but exceptionally robust and probably carrying three digits.

facts.statement: As a carnivore, Megalosaurus had a large, elongated head with long, dagger-like teeth used to slice prey flesh.
facts.quote: Being a carnivore, its large elongated head bore long dagger-like teeth to slice the flesh of its prey.

facts.statement: The skeleton of Megalosaurus was highly ossified, indicating it was robust and muscular, though its lower legs were not as heavily built as those of its relative Torvosaurus.
facts.quote: The skeleton of Megalosaurus is highly ossified, indicating a robust and muscular animal, though the lower leg was not as heavily built as that of Torvosaurus, a close relative.

facts.statement: The maxilla of Megalosaurus bears 13 teeth.
facts.quote: The maxilla bears 13 teeth.

facts.statement: The teeth of Megalosaurus were relatively large, with a crown length of up to seven centimeters.
facts.quote: The teeth are relatively large, with a crown length up to seven centimeters.

facts.statement: The cutting edges of Megalosaurus teeth bear 18 to 20 denticula per centimeter.
facts.quote: The cutting edges bear 18 to 20 denticula per centimeter.

facts.statement: The genus Megalosaurus was established by Buckland in 1824.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Buckland, 1824

facts.statement: The species M. bucklandii was described by Mantell in 1827.
facts.quote: species_authority: Mantell, 1827

facts.statement: Megalosaurus bucklandii is the only known species of the extinct genus Megalosaurus.
facts.quote: Megalosaurus bucklandii es la única especie conocida del género extinto Megalosaurus

facts.statement: Megalosaurus lived during the middle Jurassic period, approximately 166 million years ago in the Bathonian stage, in what is now Europe.
facts.quote: que vivió a mediados del período Jurásico, hace aproximadamente 166 millones de años, en el Bathoniense, en lo que hoy es Europa.

facts.statement: Buckland named the genus Megalosaurus in 1824, referring to its large size, making it the first dinosaur genus described.
facts.quote: Buckland lo nombró en 1824 como Megalosaurus, refiriéndose a su gran tamaño, convirtiéndolo en el primer género de dinosaurio descrito.

facts.statement: There is a debate regarding size estimates, with early twenty-first century trends limiting material to the lectotype resulting in lower estimates that disregard outliers of uncertain identity.
facts.quote: The trend in the early twenty-first century to limit the material to the lectotype inspired even lower estimates, disregarding outliers of uncertain identity.

facts.statement: It is debated whether certain traits identified in 2008 as autapomorphies were genuine features or the result of damage.
facts.quote: Several traits in 2008 identified as autapomorphies, later transpired to have been the result of damage.

facts.statement: A broken cervical vertebra from the New Park Quarry reveals large internal air chambers and is heavily pneumatized with large pleurocoels on its sides.
facts.quote: The breakage reveals large internal air chambers. The vertebra is also otherwise heavily pneumatized, with large pleurocoels, pneumatic excavations, on its sides.

facts.statement: Megalosaurus was a bipedal predator about 9 meters long and weighing around one tonne with a well-balanced structure for running.
facts.quote: Megalosaurus fue un depredador bípedo de unos 9 metros de largo y alrededor de una tonelada de peso con una estructura bien balanceada para la carrera.

facts.statement: The structure of its cervical vertebrae indicates that Megalosaurus had a flexible neck.
facts.quote: La estructura de las vértebras cervicales muestran que tenía un cuello flexible.

facts.statement: Like other theropods, Megalosaurus had three toes on the front of its foot and one inverted toe.
facts.quote: Como todos los terópodos, tenía tres dedos en la parte delantera del pie y uno solo invertido.

facts.statement: Megalosaurus had small forelimbs that likely possessed digits, though not as reduced as in modern theropods like Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: Aunque no habían alcanzado el tamaño minúsculo como en otros terópodos más modernos como el Tyrannosaurus, los miembros delanteros de Megalosaurus eran pequeños y tenían probablemente dígitos.

facts.statement: Megalosaurus lived in what is now Europe during the Jurassic period, between 181 and 169 million years ago, and may have hunted stegosaurs and sauropods.
facts.quote: Viviendo en lo que ahora es Europa, durante el período Jurásico, hace 181 a 169 millones de años, Megalosaurus pudo haber cazado estegosauros y saurópodos.

facts.statement: Although Megalosaurus was a large carnivore capable of attacking large sauropods, it likely supplemented its diet with scavenging.
facts.quote: Aunque Megalosaurus era un carnívoro grande y habría podido atacar probablemente incluso los saurópodos más grandes, es también probable que consiguiera algo de su alimento por el carroñeo.

facts.statement: Many bones of Megalosaurus have been recovered since the initial findings, but a complete skeleton has not yet been found.
facts.quote: Desde los primeros hallazgos, se han recuperado muchos otros huesos de Megalosaurus, sin embargo, aún no se ha encontrado un esqueleto completo.

facts.statement: Megalosaurus had the typical build of a large theropod, was bipedal, and balanced its horizontal torso with a long horizontal tail.
facts.quote: En general, Megalosaurus tenía la construcción típica de un gran terópodo. Era bípedo, el torso horizontal estaba equilibrado por una larga cola horizontal.

facts.statement: Megalosaurus had long, strong hind limbs with three weight-bearing toes and relatively short but exceptionally robust forelimbs that likely had three digits.
facts.quote: Las extremidades posteriores eran largas y fuertes con tres dedos que soportaban el peso hacia adelante, las extremidades anteriores relativamente cortas pero excepcionalmente robustas y probablemente con tres dígitos.

facts.statement: As a carnivore, Megalosaurus had a large elongated head with long dagger-like teeth for cutting the flesh of its prey.
facts.quote: Siendo un carnívoro, su gran cabeza alargada tenía largos dientes en forma de daga para cortar la carne de su presa.

facts.statement: The highly ossified skeleton of Megalosaurus indicates a robust and muscular animal, though its lower leg was not as heavily built as that of its close relative Torvosaurus.
facts.quote: El esqueleto de Megalosaurus está muy osificado, lo que indica un animal robusto y musculoso, aunque la parte inferior de la pierna no estaba tan pesadamente construida como la de Torvosaurus, un pariente cercano.

facts.statement: The upper jaw of Megalosaurus has 13 teeth.
facts.quote: El maxilar tiene 13 dientes.

facts.statement: The teeth of Megalosaurus are relatively large, with a crown length of up to 7 centimeters.
facts.quote: Los dientes son relativamente grandes, con una longitud de corona de hasta 7 centímetros.

facts.statement: The cutting edges of Megalosaurus teeth have between 18 and 20 denticles per centimeter.
facts.quote: Los bordes cortantes tienen entre 18 y 20 denticulos por centímetro.

facts.statement: The jugal bone of Megalosaurus is pneumaticized, featuring a large hole from the direction of the antorbital fenestra.
facts.quote: El hueso yugal está neumatizado, perforado por un gran agujero desde la dirección de la fenestra antorbital.

facts.statement: This level of jugal pneumaticization is unknown in other megalosaurids and may represent a separate autapomorphy.
facts.quote: Tal nivel de neumatización del yugal no se conoce de otros megalosáuridos y podría representar una autapomorfia separada.

facts.statement: The number of lower jaw teeth was probably thirteen or fourteen, although damaged preserved samples show a maximum of eleven alveoli.
facts.quote: El número de dientes dentales probablemente fue de trece o catorce, aunque las muestras dañadas conservadas muestran como máximo once alvéolos.

facts.statement: The genus Megalosaurus was named by Parkinson in 1822.
facts.quote: PBDB name: Megalosaurus (genus), Parkinson 1822

facts.statement: Megalosaurus belongs to the parent group Megalosaurinae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Megalosaurinae

facts.statement: Megalosaurus is classified in the family Megalosauridae.
facts.quote: Family: Megalosauridae

facts.statement: Megalosaurus is classified in the class Reptilia.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: The genus Megalosaurus has a recorded time range from the Rhaetian to the Maastrichtian, between 205.7 and 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Rhaetian to Maastrichtian (205.7 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: It is debated whether Megalosaurus hunted iguanodontes, as descriptions of such predation are likely inaccurate because iguanodontid skeletons are found in younger Early Cretaceous formations than the Middle Jurassic formations where Megalosaurus fossils originate.
facts.quote: Las descripciones repetidas de la caza de iguanodontes por el megalosaurio a través de los bosques que entonces cubrieron el continente son probablemente inexactas, porque los esqueletos de iguanodonte se encuentran en formaciones del Cretácico Inferior, mucho más jóvenes que las del Jurásico Medio de donde provienen los megalosaurios.

facts.statement: It is debated how large Megalosaurus was, as the lack of an articulated dorsal vertebral series makes determining an exact size difficult.
facts.quote: La falta de una serie vertebral dorsal articulada hace que sea difícil determinar un tamaño exacto.
